title: Enhancement of far-field thermal emission via polaritonic cavity modes
authors: Maelie Coral, Jose Ordonez-Miranda, Georges Hamaoui, Roman Anufriev, Laurent Jalabert, Masahiro Nomura, Yannick De Wilde, Sebastian Volz
abstract: Controlling thermal emission is crucial for applications involving thermophotovoltaics, thermal sensing, imaging, and camouflage. While prior studies focused on the emission of thermally excited guided modes (TEGMs) inside cavities, their contribution to the far-field radiation outside cavities has remained unexplored. Here, we demonstrate a tunable far-field thermal channel enabled by TEGMs arising from the coupling of surface phonon-polaritons and cavity resonances. By combining infrared emissivity experiments with fluctuational electrodynamics simulations, we identify distinct spectral features marking the conversion of two-dimensionally confined polaritonic modes into three-dimensional radiative channels. We find that silicon cavities covered with SiO2 enhance the emissivity by up to 200% near the polaritonic spectral resonance, whereas bare silicon cavities yield only broadband enhancement. These findings provide experimental evidence of TEGMs and establish a simple cavity architecture as an effective and scalable platform for tailoring thermal radiation without complex nanofabrication.
summary: The paper demonstrates that coating silicon microcavities with SiO2 significantly enhances far-field thermal emission near the polaritonic resonance. By combining emissivity measurements with advanced simulations, the authors prove this enhancement stems from thermally excited guided modes (TEGMs) efficiently coupling confined optical energy into free space radiation.
main_problem: The study aims to quantify how thermally excited guided modes (TEGMs) within optical cavities contribute to, and enhance, far-field thermal emission for applications like thermophotovoltaics.
main_result: Covering silicon cavities with a thin SiO2 layer enhances the near-infrared emissivity by up to 200% compared to bare silicon, demonstrating that TEGMs are the source of this controllable enhancement.
method: The research combines experimental measurements of hemispherical emissivity using an integrating sphere with advanced fluctuational electrodynamics simulations (SCUFF-EM).
model_or_system: The physical system is a planar cavity structure etched into Si, featuring two parallel interfaces separated by a gap. The enhancement mechanism relies on the coupling between surface phonon-polaritons and cavity resonances.
key_observables: Total hemispherical emissivity spectra ($\varepsilon(\lambda)$), and the cavity-induced Poynting vector ($\Delta P_y$) derived from simulations.
important_parameters: Cavity gap width (20 $\mu$m) and depth (160 $\mu$m); SiO2 layer thickness (60 nm); spectral resonance wavelengths (e.g., 8.5 $\mu$m).
main_assumptions: The enhancement is attributed to the conversion of two-dimensionally confined polaritonic modes into three-dimensional radiative channels via diffraction outcoupling.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images of fabricated cavities, spectral comparisons between bare and coated samples (showing peak enhancement), and spatial maps of the Poynting vector demonstrating energy channeling in the SiO2 cavity versus edge effects in bare Si.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need to study far-field emission from TEGMs. It then details the experimental setup and measurements, followed by theoretical modeling using electrodynamics simulations to decompose the emitted field into contributions from individual walls versus the hybridized cavity mode, culminating in quantitative results showing enhancement mechanisms.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, scalable platform for engineering thermal radiation spectra by controlling confined electromagnetic modes (polaritons) and their coupling to free space. This bridges concepts from cavity QED/photonics into classical thermal energy management.
